purpose: A current-controlled electronic switch. An Arduino pin can supply only 20 mA. A transistor allows a tiny 2 mA to 5 mA signal from the Arduino to switch a high-current load (up to 800 mA) like a 12V fan, piezobuzzer, solenoid, or high-power LED array in microseconds.

whenToUse.scenario: Load Draws More Than 20 mA (Buzzer, Fan, Motor, Lamp)
whenToUse.why: Connecting loads over 20 mA directly to an Arduino GPIO pin will damage the internal ATmega328P output silicon. An NPN transistor connects the load to ground safely.

whenToUse.scenario: Switching a 12V or 24V Load with a 5V Arduino
whenToUse.why: You cannot connect 12V directly to an Arduino pin. An NPN transistor acts as a low-side ground switch: 12V powers the load, and the transistor completes the circuit to ground when triggered by 5V.
whenToUse.recommended: 2N2222 or TIP120 (for higher currents up to 5A)

whenToUse.why: When a sensor outputs inverted logic (e.g. LOW when triggered, but code expects HIGH), or when you need a simple open-collector level shifter.
When your device's chassis is tied to ground and you must switch the POSITIVE voltage rail rather than the ground wire.

whenToUse.scenario: When to Choose BJT vs MOSFET
whenToUse.why: Choose a BJT (2N2222) for small loads under 500 mA (buzzers, small relays, indicators) because BJTs are dirt cheap, tiny (TO-92), and trigger reliably at just 0.7V. For heavy loads (> 1A, high-power motors, heaters, LED strips), choose a Logic-Level MOSFET instead to avoid BJT heat and base current waste.
whenToUse.recommended: BJT for < 500 mA; Logic-Level MOSFET for > 1A

basics.title: NPN vs PNP
basics.text: NPN is a 'Low-Side' switch: Emitter to GND, Collector to load negative. A HIGH signal on the Base turns it ON. PNP is a 'High-Side' switch: Emitter to VCC, Collector to load positive. A LOW signal on the Base turns it ON. NPN is used in 95% of Arduino projects.

basics.title: Always Use a Base Resistor!
basics.text: The Base-Emitter junction behaves like a forward-biased diode with a 0.7V drop. Connecting an Arduino pin directly to the Base without a resistor creates a direct short circuit, destroying the pin. Always put a 1kΩ to 4.7kΩ resistor between the Arduino pin and the Base.

basics.title: Saturation (Switching) vs Active Region (Amplification)
basics.text: In digital Arduino projects, we operate the transistor in 'Saturation': driving enough current into the Base so the Collector-Emitter junction turns FULLY ON with minimal resistance (voltage drop ~0.2V).

basics.title: Base Resistor Formula
basics.text: Rb = (V_arduino - 0.7V) / I_base. If your load needs 200 mA and the transistor gain (beta) is 30 in saturation, you need ~6.6 mA base current: (5V - 0.7V) / 0.0066A ≈ 650 Ω. A standard 1 kΩ resistor is perfect for most common switching tasks.

types.name: NPN Bipolar Junction Transistor
types.trigger: Active-HIGH (Current into Base turns it ON)
types.looks: Classic small black half-cylinder (TO-92) with 3 legs: Emitter, Base, Collector.
pros: Turns on with standard 5V or 3.3V GPIO
Cheap and included in every kit
cons: Small saturation voltage drop (Vce ~0.2V–0.3V) wastes a bit of power
Requires continuous base current to stay ON

types.name: PNP Bipolar Junction Transistor
types.trigger: Active-LOW (Pulling Base lower than Emitter turns it ON)
types.looks: Same black TO-92 package; look for part numbers starting with 2N3906, BC557, or PN2907.
pros: Keeps the load referenced to true ground at all times
cons: Cannot directly switch voltages higher than 5V from an Arduino pin without an extra NPN pre-driver stage

types.name: Darlington Pair (e.g. TIP120)
types.looks: Larger black TO-220 package with metal mounting tab with hole.
pros: Huge current gain (hFE > 1000) requires under 5 mA from Arduino pin to switch 3A to 5A loads
Handles higher power than standard TO-92
cons: Higher saturation voltage drop (~1.2V to 2V) generates noticeable heat under load
uses: Solenoid valves and mechanical door strikes

commonParts.whenToUse: The workhorse NPN transistor for Arduino kits. Best for buzzers, relays, small 5V/12V motors.
Low-current general-purpose switching, logic inverters, and signal level shifting.
Complement to 2N3904. Used for high-side switching and H-bridge directional circuits.
European standard small-signal NPN. Very high gain, excellent for audio and sensitive triggers.
Driving beefy 12V motors, solenoids, or actuators when a MOSFET is unavailable.
